title: Proteolysis-targeting chimeras with reduced off-targets
abstract: Proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) are molecules that induce proximity between target proteins and E3 ligases triggering target protein degradation. Pomalidomide, a widely used E3 ligase recruiter in PROTACs, can independently degrade other proteins, including zinc-finger (ZF) proteins, with vital roles in health and disease. This off-target degradation hampers the therapeutic applicability of pomalidomide-based PROTACs, requiring development of PROTAC design rules that minimize off-target degradation. Here we developed a high-throughput platform that interrogates off-target degradation and found that reported pomalidomide-based PROTACs induce degradation of several ZF proteins. We generated a library of pomalidomide analogues to understand how functionalizing different positions of the phthalimide ring, hydrogen bonding, and steric and hydrophobic effects impact ZF protein degradation. Modifications of appropriate size on the C5 position reduced off-target ZF degradation, which we validated through target engagement and proteomics studies. By applying these design principles, we developed anaplastic lymphoma kinase oncoprotein-targeting PROTACs with enhanced potency and minimal off-target degradation.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This 2023 Nature Chemistry article has been taken up strongly in the scholarly record, with 109 citations and field- and year-normalized standing in the top 1% of its cohort. Its influence is concentrated in protein degradation and medicinal chemistry, where it is already being used as a reference point for follow-on work on PROTAC design and on reducing cereblon-related off-target effects.

Full narrative

The article addresses a practical bottleneck in PROTAC development: pomalidomide, a widely used cereblon recruiter, can drive unwanted degradation of zinc-finger proteins and other off-targets. By focusing on this design problem, the paper speaks directly to a major concern in targeted protein degradation and offers guidance that is relevant to both mechanistic studies and therapeutic design. The work is also openly accessible through green open access, which likely supports its visibility and reuse.

The citation record shows clear and sustained scholarly uptake. OpenAlex records 109 citations, and the article is ranked in the top 1% for its field and publication year. The citing landscape is broad but especially active in medicinal chemistry and related drug-discovery venues, with repeated citation in Journal of Medicinal Chemistry, European Journal of Medicinal Chemistry, and other journals working on protein degradation, ubiquitin biology, and bifunctional molecules. The presence of reviews among the citing works suggests that the paper is not only being used in primary research but is also helping frame synthesis across the area.

The surrounding discourse is more modest than the citation record but still visible. Crossref event data captured news discussion from Phys.org, and Reddit shows at least one community mention. Scite also records citation statements that are predominantly mentioning rather than strongly supporting, which is consistent with a paper that is being cited as a methodological or conceptual reference point while its specific claims are incorporated into a broader and fast-moving literature.

The downstream reuse profile reinforces that interpretation. The work appears in a wide range of later articles, preprints, and reviews, with follow-on publications spanning protein degradation, ubiquitin-proteasome pathways, and adjacent drug-discovery topics. The citing institutions and countries are distributed across a substantial international network, with especially visible activity in the United States, China, Germany, and the United Kingdom. Overall, the record portrays a highly influential methods-and-design paper whose impact is centered on shaping how researchers think about cereblon-based degrader selectivity and off-target control.

The authorship is anchored at the Broad Institute and Harvard University, and the paper is supported by multiple NIH awards, including cancer, biomedical imaging, and general medical sciences funding. That funding profile is consistent with the translational relevance of the topic: a chemistry-driven strategy aimed at making protein degraders more precise and more viable for future therapeutic use.
